lines.text: Every group has a song in it. But making one together takes instruments, a studio, and weeks.
A.I. music tools help one person, typing one prompt. The song belongs to the prompt, not the people.
This is CrowdChorus. One room. Many voices. One original song.
A host picks a nickname, a mood, and a theme, and opens a room.
Friends join from their phones, with a six letter code or the Q.R. code. No accounts. No installs.
The room gets one original chorus line, so everyone sings the same words in the same key.
A pitch guide plays the melody. Then a four beat count in, and six seconds to sing.
Preview it, retry it, and nothing joins the mix until you agree.
The host watches the roster fill in live. Three browsers, three voices.
Finalize. Even a double click creates exactly one job. A Post gress unique index guarantees it.
Everyone watches six honest steps. The cover shows up the moment it exists.
And here's the reveal.
That's our three singers, over the backing, mixed on this laptop in two seconds.
Music models make instrumentals from text. They can't take a crowd's recordings. So we built the human part ourselves.
Every clip is decoded with F F mpeg and analyzed in Rust, with the YIN pitch detector written in C.
Each voice is filtered, aligned to the downbeat and loudness matched, then bussed through a free verb reverb in C plus plus.
The backing ducks under the chorus. And a test proves that removing any one voice changes the mix.
Five languages, one repo, and no network calls between them. They meet at Post gress rows, files, and command line tools.
TypeScript runs the room. Python runs the generation worker. Ruby runs migrations and voice clip cleanup.
Post gress listen and notify wakes the worker and streams live updates. Events land in a Timescale hypertable, the engine behind Tiger Data.
Every sponsor tool is a provider plug in, switched on by one environment variable.
Gemini writes the chorus line and the creative brief, as schema validated output.
Nah no Banana paints an abstract album cover.
Lyria composes the instrumental in the room's key and tempo.
Nimble searches the theme for inspiration.
Snowflake runs the analytics across every room.
And Sentry catches errors, without ever seeing audio, names, or lyrics.
In this recording no keys are set, so each step runs a local fallback, and the page labels it. Nothing pretends to be generated.
It works end to end. Four test suites and a three browser Playwright run, all green in CI.
Voices stay private, never get a public link, and are deleted after twenty four hours.
Our stretch: browser audio capture, signal processing in three languages, and Post gress as a message bus.
CrowdChorus. One room. Many voices. One original song.
It's open source. Clone it, and sing.
